index.title: Which Fix Raises F1 More
index.prompt: A classifier has TP = 40, FP = 40 and FN = 20 on a validation set. Fix A turns ten false negatives into true positives and fix B turns ten false positives into true negatives. Which of the two raises F1 more?
index.answer: Fix A, because its ten corrected predictions become true positives, which F1 counts in its numerator as well as its denominator. Both fixes cut the error term (FP + FN) / 2 from 30 to 25. Fix A also adds 10 true positives, and TP sits in the numerator of F1 = TP / (TP + (FP + FN) / 2) as well as the denominator, while the true negatives fix B creates never enter F1. So fix A gives 50 / (50 + 25) = 0.667 against 40 / (40 + 25) = 0.615 for fix B, both up from 40 / 70 = 0.571. Fix B raises precision further (0.571 against 0.556), but fix A also lifts recall from 0.667 to 0.833.

theory.title: Confusion Matrices, Precision, Recall, and F1
overview: Compute accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 from one confusion matrix, and show why accuracy is the wrong metric on imbalanced data.

setup.p: A binary classifier is evaluated on $1000$ examples, producing the confusion matrix

prompt.p: Compute the accuracy, precision, and recall of this classifier.

answer.p: Substituting the four counts:

The mnemonic for which denominator is which: precision is measured over everything the model *flagged* (the predicted-positive column), recall over everything that actually *is* positive (the true-positive row). Precision answers "when it fires, how often is it right?" Recall answers "of the things it should have caught, how many did it?"

prompt.p: The classifier above is $90\%$ accurate. Compute the accuracy of the trivial classifier that predicts $\hat{y} = 0$ for every example, and explain what this shows.

answer.p: The positive class has $\text{TP} + \text{FN} = 50$ members out of $1000$, so it is $5\%$ of the data. Predicting $0$ always gets every negative right and every positive wrong:

The trivial classifier is *more accurate* than the trained one, while being completely useless: it has recall $0$ and precision undefined. This shows that accuracy on imbalanced data is dominated by the majority class and can be maximized by ignoring the minority class entirely.

The trained classifier is genuinely better at the task that matters: it catches $80\%$ of the positives. Accuracy simply cannot see that, because the $40$ true positives it adds are outnumbered by the $90$ false positives it introduces, and accuracy weights both equally.

The lesson is to always compare against the majority-class baseline. If your accuracy does not beat it by a meaningful margin, your model has learned nothing useful, and the official USAAIO problems' use of macro-$F_1$ rather than accuracy is precisely to close this loophole.

prompt.p: The $F_1$ score is the harmonic mean of precision $P$ and recall $R$:
Compute $F_1$ for this classifier, and explain why the harmonic mean is used rather than the arithmetic mean.

answer.p: Why harmonic. The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller of the two values, so it punishes imbalance between precision and recall. The arithmetic mean here would be $0.554$, noticeably more flattering.

The difference matters most at the extremes. A classifier that predicts positive for everything has $R = 1$ and, on this data, $P = 0.05$. Its arithmetic mean is a respectable-looking $0.525$. Its $F_1$ is

correctly identifying it as useless. Since either metric can be trivially maxed out alone (predict everything positive for perfect recall, or predict only your single most confident example for near-perfect precision), a summary metric must refuse to reward one at the total expense of the other, and the harmonic mean does that.

prompt.p: Under which circumstances is the $F_1$ score generally preferred over classification accuracy?

choices: A. When the dataset is very large.
B. When the classes are well balanced.
C. When the model is linear.
D. When the dataset is highly imbalanced.
E. When the number of features is large.

answer.p: Part 2 is the argument: on imbalanced data, accuracy is dominated by the majority class and a degenerate classifier can beat a useful one. $F_1$ depends only on TP, FP, and FN. It never uses TN, the count that the majority class inflates, so it cannot be gamed by predicting the majority everywhere.

The other options are irrelevant to the choice. Dataset size affects the *variance* of any metric, not which one is appropriate. Balanced classes are the case where accuracy is fine, and neither model family nor feature count bears on the question. Note also that $F_1$ is asymmetric by design, swapping which class you call positive changes it, so you must define the positive class as the one you care about detecting.

answer.result: D. When the dataset is highly imbalanced.

prompt.p: Relate precision to the Bayes computation of a diagnostic test's positive predictive value by expressing it in terms of the prevalence $\pi = P(y = 1)$, the true positive rate $\text{TPR}$, and the false positive rate $\text{FPR}$.

answer.p: Precision is exactly the posterior $P(y = 1 \mid \hat{y} = 1)$. Applying Bayes' rule with the law of total probability in the denominator,
Check against the data: $\text{TPR} = 40/50 = 0.8$, $\text{FPR} = 90/950 \approx 0.0947$, $\pi = 0.05$, giving

The important structural fact is that TPR and FPR are properties of the *classifier* alone, they condition on the true label and are invariant to prevalence, whereas precision depends on $\pi$ as well. This is the same phenomenon as a base-rate shift: the test did not change, only the population did.

Two practical consequences. A model with excellent precision in a balanced development set can have terrible precision in deployment where the positive class is rare, with no change to the model. And ROC curves (TPR against FPR) are prevalence-invariant, whereas precision-recall curves are not, which is why PR curves are the more informative choice for rare-event detection, and ROC-AUC can look deceptively good there.

prompt.p: Explain what macro-averaged $F_1$ means for a $C$-class problem, why the official USAAIO problems use it, and how it differs from micro-averaging.

answer.p: Macro-$F_1$ computes $F_1$ separately for each class, treating that class as positive and all others as negative, then takes the unweighted mean:

Micro-averaging instead pools the counts across classes first, summing all TP, FP, and FN, and computes a single $F_1$ from the totals. In single-label multiclass classification, micro-$F_1$ equals accuracy.

The difference is the weighting. Micro-averaging weights each *example* equally, so large classes dominate. Macro-averaging weights each *class* equally, so a class with $20$ examples counts as much as one with $20{,}000$. A model that ignores a rare class entirely gets $F_1^{(c)} = 0$ for it, which drags the macro average down hard, while barely moving the micro average.

That is exactly why the official problems grade on macro-$F_1$: it removes the incentive to optimize the majority class and forces contestants to handle every class. It is also why the baseline for a balanced binary task is quoted at about $0.5$: random guessing achieves roughly that.

parts.requirement: Do not use scikit-learn and do not use any loop.

prompt.p: Run the following starter code:
Compute TP, FP, FN, TN and then precision, recall, and $F_1$ without any library metric function. Guard against division by zero.

lines: precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0

answer.p: The boolean masks combine with $\texttt{\&}$ (elementwise), not $\texttt{and}$ (which would try to evaluate whole arrays as truth values and raise). Summing a boolean array counts the $\texttt{True}$ entries, so all four cells come out in four vectorized passes.
For this data: $\text{TP} = 3$, $\text{FP} = 2$, $\text{FN} = 1$, $\text{TN} = 4$, giving

The zero guards are not pedantry. A model that predicts no positives at all gives $\text{TP} + \text{FP} = 0$ and an undefined precision. Without the guard you get a $\texttt{nan}$ that silently propagates into a macro average and destroys the whole score. The convention of returning $0$ matches scikit-learn's $\texttt{zero\_division=0}$.

theory.title: The Threshold F2 Picks
overview: A model inspects welds on a production line and flags the ones it scores as faulty. A weld is flagged when its score is at least the threshold $t$. Ten welds from a validation batch, four of them faulty, sorted by score:

setup.p: Use only the ten scores as candidate thresholds. Recall that $F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2) PR / (\beta^2 P + R)$, where $P$ is precision and $R$ is recall.

prompt.p: Which threshold maximizes $F_1$?

answer.p: Setting $t$ to the $k$-th score flags the top $k$ welds. With $TP_k$ faulty welds among them, $FP = k - TP_k$ and $FN = 4 - TP_k$, so the denominator of the count form collapses:
The maximum is $6/8 = 0.75$ at $k = 4$, so $t = 0.71$: three of the four faulty welds caught with one false alarm.

prompt.p: Which threshold maximizes $F_2$?

answer.p: Substitute $P = TP_k / k$ and $R = TP_k / 4$ into $F_2 = 5PR / (4P + R)$ and multiply the top and bottom by $4k / TP_k$:
The maximum is $20/24 = 0.833$ at $k = 8$, so $t = 0.38$: all four faulty welds caught with four false alarms.

prompt.p: Explain, using the two formulas in terms of $k$, why $F_2$ chose the lower threshold, and say when a grader would rather compute $F_2$ than $F_1$.

answer.p: Both formulas have the form $(1 + \beta^2)\,TP_k / (k + \beta^2 \cdot 4)$. Each extra flag adds 1 to the denominator in both, but the fixed part of the denominator is 4 for $F_1$ and 16 for $F_2$, so one more flag costs $F_2$ a smaller fraction of its value. Going from $k = 4$ to $k = 8$ adds one true positive and four flags: $F_1$ falls from $6/8$ to $8/12$, while $F_2$ rises from $15/20$ to $20/24$.

$\beta = 2$ weights recall four times as much as precision, so $F_2$ is the grader's choice when a miss costs much more than a false alarm. A faulty weld that ships is far more expensive than a sound weld inspected twice.

theory.title: The Flags a Lower Threshold Adds
overview: A streaming service scores every subscriber by how likely they are to cancel next month, and sends a retention offer to each subscriber scoring at least $t$. Last month 400 of its 10,000 subscribers cancelled, and the team measured three thresholds on that month:

setup.p: Count only the two kinds of mistake. An offer sent to a subscriber who would have stayed wastes 1 unit, and a subscriber who cancels without having had an offer costs 2 units. An offer sent to a subscriber who would have cancelled keeps them and costs nothing.

prompt.p: Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 adds an offer for every subscriber who scores at least 0.3 but below 0.5. What fraction of those subscribers cancelled? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: Turn each row into counts. Recall times the 400 cancellers gives the true positives, and the true positives divided by the precision give the number of offers. At $t = 0.5$, for example, $TP = 0.70 \times 400 = 280$ and there are $280 / 0.80 = 350$ offers. The wasted offers are the offers minus TP, and the missed cancellers are 400 minus TP:
The move from 0.5 to 0.3 adds $500 - 350 = 150$ offers and $320 - 280 = 40$ true positives, so

The 0.64 at $t = 0.3$ averages two groups: the first 350 offers, right 280 times, and the new 150, right 40 times, $(280 + 40) / 500$. The same subtraction for the move from 0.8 to 0.5 gives 100 cancellers among 150 new offers, $0.667$, so each step down the threshold reaches subscribers the model is less sure of.

prompt.p: Which of the three thresholds gives the lowest total cost?

answer.p: The total is $1 \cdot FP + 2 \cdot FN$, with the counts from Part 1:

The lowest is 310, at $t = 0.5$. Going down from 0.8 to 0.5 catches 100 more cancellers, saving 200 units, for 50 more wasted offers, costing 50. Going down from 0.5 to 0.3 catches only 40 more, saving 80 units, for 110 more wasted offers, costing 110.

prompt.p: A teammate argues for $t = 0.3$: its precision is still 0.64, so nearly two of every three extra offers reach a subscriber who would have cancelled, and a missed canceller costs twice a wasted offer. Say what is wrong with the argument. Then find the cost of a missed canceller, in units, above which moving from 0.5 to 0.3 does lower the total.

answer.p: The 0.64 is the precision of all 500 offers made at $t = 0.3$. The decision is about the 150 offers that the move adds, and Part 1 showed that only 40 of them reach a subscriber who would cancel. The cumulative precision hides how poor the new offers are, because the 350 offers kept from $t = 0.5$ make up most of it.
With a missed canceller costing $c$ units, the move catches 40 more cancellers, saving $40c$, and wastes 110 more units on offers, so it pays when

At $c = 2$ the move loses 30 units, as Part 2 found. The teammate's reading would put the break-even point at $0.36 / 0.64 \approx 0.56$, nearly five times too low. To judge a move of the threshold, compare the true and false positives that the move adds, not the precision at the new threshold.

prompt.p: A model sorts 100 support tickets into billing, technical and legal. Its confusion matrix, with true classes on rows and predictions on columns, is
It never predicts legal. What is its macro-F1?

choices.explain: That is the micro average. Pooling the counts gives 90 true positives, 10 false positives and 10 false negatives, so micro-F1 = 90 / 100, the accuracy. The 10 legal tickets are only a tenth of that score, while macro-F1 hands legal a full third.
That is the weighted average, which weights each class F1 by its 50, 40 and 10 tickets: 0.5(0.909) + 0.4(1) + 0.1(0) = 0.855. Macro-F1 weights the three classes equally.

This scores billing as perfect. Its recall is 1, but the 10 legal tickets it received are false positives for billing, so its precision is 50/60 and its F1 is 0.909, not 1. With that fixed the average is 0.636.

Billing has 50 true positives and the 10 legal tickets as false positives, so its F1 is 2(50) / (2(50) + 10) = 10/11 = 0.909. Technical is perfect, F1 = 1. Legal has no true positives, so its F1 is 0 / (0 + 10/2) = 0. The macro average gives each class a third: (0.909 + 1 + 0) / 3 = 7/11 = 0.636.

theory.title: The ROC Curve of Hard Predictions
overview: A classifier outputs only hard labels, 0 or 1. On a test set of 40 positives and 160 negatives it flags 32 of the positives and 48 of the negatives. Passed to `roc_auc_score` in place of scores, the labels still produce a number. Treated as scores they allow only three distinct thresholds, so the ROC curve joins three points with straight segments: $(0, 0)$ when nothing is flagged, the classifier's own $(\text{FPR}, \text{TPR})$, and $(1, 1)$ when everything is flagged.

prompt.p: Compute the area under this ROC curve.

answer.p: $\text{TPR} = 32/40 = 0.8$ and $\text{FPR} = 48/160 = 0.3$, so the curve runs $(0, 0) \to (0.3, 0.8) \to (1, 1)$. Split the area at $x = 0.3$: a triangle on the left and a trapezoid on the right.

prompt.p: For a hard classifier with true positive rate $a$ and false positive rate $b$, show that the area under this three-point curve equals the balanced accuracy, $\tfrac12(\text{TPR} + \text{TNR})$, where $\text{TNR} = 1 - \text{FPR}$ is the specificity.

answer.p: The same split at $x = b$ gives a triangle of area $\tfrac12 ab$ and a trapezoid of width $1 - b$ between heights $a$ and $1$:
For the classifier above, $\tfrac12(0.8 + 0.7) = 0.75$, as in Part 1. $\qquad\blacksquare$

prompt.p: The AUC also equals the share of positive-negative pairs that the scores put in the right order, with a tied pair counting one half. Compute that fraction for the hard classifier with rates $a$ and $b$, and show that it agrees with Part 2.

answer.p: A pair is one positive and one negative. The positive is flagged in a fraction $a$ of pairs and the negative in a fraction $b$, independently, since every positive meets every negative. That gives three kinds of pair:

list: Right when the positive is flagged and the negative is not: $a(1 - b)$.
Tied when both are flagged or neither is: $ab + (1 - a)(1 - b)$.
Wrong when the negative is flagged and the positive is not: $(1 - a)b$.

answer.p: So the pair fraction is

which is the area from Part 2. With the counts above: of the $40 \times 160 = 6400$ pairs, $32 \times 112 = 3584$ are right and $32 \times 48 + 8 \times 112 = 2432$ are tied, giving $(3584 + 1216) / 6400 = 0.75$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

prompt.p: A grader scores submitted 0/1 labels by balanced accuracy. A teammate reports AUC 0.75 for this classifier and AUC 0.86 for a logistic regression, computed from its predicted probabilities, and concludes that the logistic regression will score higher with the grader. Explain why the two AUCs do not support that conclusion, and say what to compute instead.

answer.p: The grader sees labels, so the logistic regression will be judged at one threshold, exactly like the first classifier. By Part 2, the AUC of a set of 0/1 labels is its balanced accuracy, so the first classifier's 0.75 is already the score the grader would give it on this data.

The 0.86 is the area under the logistic regression's full curve, swept over every threshold. It gives credit for ordering examples within what will become its 0s and within what will become its 1s, and the grader never sees that ordering once a threshold has turned probabilities into labels. The logistic regression's balanced accuracy at the threshold it submits can be well below 0.86, and nothing in the two AUCs says whether it will beat 0.75.

Put both models in the form the grader sees. Choose the logistic regression's threshold on validation, turn its probabilities into 0/1 labels, and compute the balanced accuracy of both sets of labels on the same validation data. Those two numbers estimate the two scores the grader will give.

prompt.p: What is its precision on the validation set? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: Each ROC coordinate is a rate within one class: the true positive rate divides by the counterfeit listings and the false positive rate by the genuine ones. Changing how many listings of each class there are leaves both rates alone, provided each class scores the way it did in validation.

Precision divides by the flags, and the flags mix the two classes in a proportion the base rate sets. With 450 genuine listings per counterfeit one, a false positive rate of 0.05 already produces 22.5 false flags for every 0.9 true ones.
The reviewers open flags, so the precision-recall curve describes their work: at recall 0.90 they find a counterfeit in about 1 flag in 26.

theory.title: Ranking a Week of Claims
overview: An insurer receives nine claims in one week, and two models rank that batch. Investigation later shows that four of the nine were fraudulent. From the top of each ranking down:

setup.p: Two teams use the ranking of each week's batch. A fraud investigator opens only the two claims ranked highest in the batch. A review team must catch every fraud in the batch, so it opens claims from the top until it reaches the last fraudulent one, and the number of claims it opens is what the review costs.

prompt.p: Which model should the investigator use, and does the AUC agree?

answer.p: In its top two, model A has one fraud, since its first claim is genuine, and model B has two. The investigator should use model B.
For the AUC, pair each of the 4 frauds with each of the 5 genuine claims: 20 pairs, each worth $1/20$.

list: Model A: the genuine claim at rank 1 sits above all four frauds, and each fraud sits above the four genuine claims at ranks 6 to 9. $\text{AUC} = 16/20 = 0.80$.
Model B: the frauds at ranks 1, 2, 5 and 8 sit above 5, 5, 3 and 1 genuine claims. $\text{AUC} = 14/20 = 0.70$.

answer.p: The AUC prefers model A, so it disagrees. Every pair counts the same $1/20$, wherever the two claims sit. All four of model A's wrong pairs involve its rank 1 claim, the first claim the investigator opens. Model B has six wrong pairs: the genuine claims at ranks 3 and 4 each sit above the frauds at ranks 5 and 8, and the genuine claims at ranks 6 and 7 each sit above the fraud at rank 8. None of them involves the top two claims, so none changes what the investigator sees. The investigator's own number is the count of frauds in the top two.

prompt.p: Suppose the investigator could open the top $k$ claims of the batch, for any $k$ from 1 to 9. For how many values of $k$ does model A find more frauds than model B? What does the pattern say about choosing between the two models when the budget is fixed?

answer.p: Count the frauds among the top $k$ claims of each ranking:
Model A finds more for $k = 4$ to $7$, four values. Model B is ahead at $k = 1$ and $2$, and the two tie at 3, 8 and 9.

So neither model is better at every budget. With $k$ claims opened, precision is the frauds found over $k$ and recall is the frauds found over 4, so at a fixed $k$ the model with more frauds is better on both, and the choice comes down to one count at that $k$. Fix the budget first, then compare the models there: model B for one or two claims a week, model A for four to seven. The AUC is one number for the whole ranking and does not say which $k$ it describes.

prompt.p: Which model should the review use? Does a higher AUC always mean a cheaper review? Show that it does, or give two rankings of nine claims, four of them fraudulent, where the ranking with the higher AUC makes the review open more claims.

answer.p: The review stops at the last fraud: rank 5 in model A's list, 5 claims of which 1 is genuine, and rank 8 in model B's, 8 claims of which 4 are genuine. The review should use model A, which also has the higher AUC.

That agreement is not guaranteed. The cost of the review is the rank of the last fraud, which depends on one claim, while the AUC averages all 20 pairs. Write F for a fraud and G for a genuine claim, from rank 1 down, so model A is G F F F F G G G G. Take the ranking F F F G G F G G G. The frauds at ranks 1, 2 and 3 each sit above all 5 genuine claims and the fraud at rank 6 above 3, so its AUC is $18/20 = 0.90$, higher than model A's 0.80. Its review opens 6 claims, more than model A's 5. In the same way, F F F G G G G G F has an AUC of $15/20 = 0.75$, above model B's 0.70, with a review of all 9 claims against model B's 8.

Each job has its own number: the frauds in the top two for the investigator, and the rank of the last fraud for the review. The AUC averages all 20 pairs and answers neither question directly. Here it agrees with the review and disagrees with the investigator.

prompt.p: A classifier has $TP = 40$, $FP = 40$ and $FN = 20$ on a validation set. You can make one of two fixes, and each changes ten predictions.

list: **Fix A.** Ten of the missed positives are now flagged: ten false negatives become true positives.
**Fix B.** Ten of the false alarms are no longer flagged: ten false positives become true negatives.

prompt.p: Which fix raises F1 more?

choices.text: Fix B, because precision is the smaller of the two numbers and F1 leans toward the smaller one
choices.explain: Precision, 40 / 80 = 0.50, is indeed the smaller number, and the harmonic mean leans toward it. But fix A raises precision too, to 50 / 90 = 0.556, while lifting recall from 0.667 to 0.833. Fix B lifts only precision, to 0.571, so fix A ends higher: 0.667 against 0.615.

choices.text: Neither: they give the same F1, because F1 weights false positives and false negatives equally
choices.explain: False positives and false negatives do carry equal weight in the denominator, so both fixes cut the error term from 30 to 25. The difference is where the ten predictions go: fix A turns them into true positives, which F1 counts, and fix B into true negatives, which F1 never uses. So fix A ends higher, 0.667 against 0.615.

choices.text: Fix A, because its ten corrected predictions become true positives, which F1 counts in its numerator as well as its denominator
choices.explain: Both fixes cut the error term (FP + FN) / 2 from 30 to 25. Fix A also adds 10 true positives, and TP sits in the numerator of F1 = TP / (TP + (FP + FN) / 2) as well as the denominator, while the true negatives fix B creates never enter F1. So fix A gives 50 / (50 + 25) = 0.667 against 40 / (40 + 25) = 0.615 for fix B, both up from 40 / 70 = 0.571. Fix B raises precision further (0.571 against 0.556), but fix A also lifts recall from 0.667 to 0.833.

answer.p: Both fixes cut the error term (FP + FN) / 2 from 30 to 25. Fix A also adds 10 true positives, and TP sits in the numerator of F1 = TP / (TP + (FP + FN) / 2) as well as the denominator, while the true negatives fix B creates never enter F1. So fix A gives 50 / (50 + 25) = 0.667 against 40 / (40 + 25) = 0.615 for fix B, both up from 40 / 70 = 0.571. Fix B raises precision further (0.571 against 0.556), but fix A also lifts recall from 0.667 to 0.833.

answer.result: Fix A, because its ten corrected predictions become true positives, which F1 counts in its numerator as well as its denominator
